value: did not respond to predator odour (no response to fox or cat urine on dowels at foraging stations)

source.authors: Emma E. Spencer, Mathew S. Crowther, Christopher R. Dickman
source.title: Risky Business: Do Native Rodents Use Habitat and Odor Cues to Manage Predation Risk in Australian Deserts?

method: field experiment: paired food bowls (open sand vs shrub or spinifex) at foraging stations with predator-urine dowels versus untreated control dowels; bowl visits, giving-up density and movement tracks
conditions: Wild spinifex hopping-mouse at Ethabuka Reserve, Simpson Desert, Australia; two field experiments run in sequence at night under a new moon; no captive animals. Experiment 1: fox urine versus no urine, 56 foraging stations at three sites, 3 nights of odour after 3 nights of pre-baiting. Experiment 2: fox urine, cat urine or no urine, 32 stations at two sites, 5 nights of odour after 7 nights of pre-baiting. Odour treatments alternated between stations; randomisation not described; control dowels untreated, no pungency control. Fox urine was syringed from the bladders of foxes killed for pest control and stored at about 1 C until use; cat urine came from euthanized cats collected from the RSPCA; dowel tops were soaked overnight in urine (volume not stated), and extra urine was applied at dusk each night (Discussion). Fox and cat are introduced predators, and the authors offer the lack of a shared evolutionary history with these newly invasive predators as one explanation of the null. In Experiment 1 one burnt and one unburnt dune crest was sampled at each site (about 25% of the reserve burnt in 2011), and macrohabitat entered five of the top movement models (more use of open sand, spinifex and shrub in burnt habitat). Individuals were identified from footprints each morning and the number of individual N. alexis is not reported (152 tracks followed in Experiment 1, 319 in Experiment 2). Mean giving-up density was 18.6 +/- 0.1 SE (n = 175) and 18.1 +/- 0.1 SE (n = 279) peanut quarters left of 20, invariant across odour treatments; odour appeared in no Experiment 2 movement model and in one Experiment 1 movement model with standard error larger than its estimate; the text gives no F or P values for odour (Table 1 not read). The only significant foraging effect reported was habitat: in Experiment 2 mice visited open microhabitats more than sheltered ones (Z = 1.77, P = 0.048). Methods do not say whether other rodent species visited the stations; only N. alexis is reported. The null concerns odour on a dowel next to food, so it does not show the mice cannot detect the urine.
quote: Rodents did not respond to predator odor, perhaps reflecting the inconsistent selection pressure that is imposed on prey species in the desert environment due to the transience of predator-presence.

value: bycatch of green sea turtles 59.5% lower in gillnets lit with green LEDs than in unlit control nets
units: categorical (percent reduction in bycatch per unit effort, illuminated vs control net)

source.authors: Dwi Ariyoga Gautama, Hendro Susanto, Mochammad Riyanto, Ronny I. Wahju, Michael Osmond, John H. Wang
source.title: Reducing sea turtle bycatch with net illumination in an Indonesian small-scale coastal gillnet fishery

method: paired field experiment in a commercial fishery: illuminated versus unlit control gillnets fished on the same nights; Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test
conditions: Wild green turtles caught as bycatch off Paloh, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, and released alive; April 2014 to June 2017. 70 pairs of control and illuminated nets (140 nets), fished the same night 1 to 2 km apart. Lights were constant (non-flashing) green LEDs, peak 500 nm, every 10 m on the floatline; light intensity not reported; whether net assignment or side was randomised is not stated. Green turtles: 14 in control nets and 6 in illuminated nets, Wilcoxon p = 0.039 (test statistic not reported). Other species in the same experiment had very small counts: olive ridley 7 vs 1 and hawksbill 3 vs 2 (all turtles 24 vs 9; multi-species reduction 61.4% per the abstract, 60.7% in the Discussion). Catch per unit effort of total catch and target species remained similar between treatments (total marketable catch p = 0.370, target catch p = 0.096, non-target catch p = 0.655). Nets were set in late afternoon and soaked overnight (mean 12.4 h control, 12.1 h illuminated), 203 mm stretched mesh, about 1.2 km long; onboard observers recorded catch. Mean green turtle CPUE was 0.18 +/- 0.05 SE in control nets and 0.07 +/- 0.03 in illuminated nets (Table 3 prints 0.7, apparently a typo). The experiment compares nets, not animals: an effect of the lights on turtles is inferred by the authors, and the study cannot separate visual avoidance from other responses to the lit net.
quote: Results indicated that net illumination significantly reduced multi-species sea turtle bycatch by 61.4% and specifically green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas) by 59.5%, while the CPUE of total catch and target species remained similar.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in three abutting pieces, end verified. Eyed animal responding to light, so filed under behaviour_vision. value: no significant reduction in the proportion of sharks interacting with a bait while a commercial electric anklet deterrent was active
units: categorical (null result; proportion interacting with bait, active vs inactive device)

source.authors: Channing A. Egeberg, Ryan M. Kempster, Nathan S. Hart, Laura Ryan, Lucille Chapuis, Caroline C. Kerr, Carl Schmidt, Enrico Gennari, Kara E. Yopak, Shaun P. Collin
source.title: Not all electric shark deterrents are made equal: Effects of a commercial electric anklet deterrent on white shark behaviour

method: field experiment with stereo-video rigs: baited target with an active versus an inactive (visually identical, uncharged) electric anklet deterrent (Electronic Shark Defense System)
conditions: Free-ranging wild white sharks (estimated 2 to 4 m) at Seal Island, Mossel Bay, South Africa, July 2014. 395 encounters (238 control, 157 active) from 44 individual sharks, 51 h of footage; 17 control and 17 active deployments of 90 min each. Bait: a PVC canister with about 0.5 kg of sardines and fish heads suspended 1 m in front of the cameras, so the sharks also had chemical and visual cues, and the test measures the device against a bait rather than isolating the electric sense. Four rigs deployed at once at sites at least 300 m apart and rotated among sites; starting location randomly assigned; treatments spread evenly over locations and time slots. The device discharged at 7.8 Hz for 2.5 s then was inactive for 2.6 s, so many sharks met it in the inactive state. On first encounter 43.5 +/- 10.6% of individuals interacted with the bait in control trials and 33.3 +/- 10.5% in active trials (the null filed here). At close proximity (under 15.5 cm) the active device did reduce the number of sharks biting the bait (52.4% of individuals in active trials against 87.0% in control; test in Table 2, not read), countered by an increase in other, less aggressive interactions (Discussion: Bites down 34.6%, Bumps up 24.6%). The device's field was measured with a voltage-gradient probe at set distances and angles; no field value is filed here. No individual shark was identified in more than one trial, though the authors cannot be certain. In control trials the sharks' proximity decreased with each subsequent approach, and in active trials the proximity difference was negatively correlated with the number of encounters, which the authors read as some habituation. The authors judge the effective range very short and the effect unreliable.
quote: We found that the ESDS had limited meaningful effect on the behaviour of C. carcharias, with no significant reduction in the proportion of sharks interacting with the bait in the presence of the active device.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in three abutting pieces ('...with no significant reduction' | 'in the proportion of sharks interacting with the bait' | 'in the presence of the active device.'), end verified. value: repelled on first encounter with an active electric deterrent at a mean proximity of 131 cm, corresponding to a mean voltage gradient of 9.7 V/m
units: cm (mean proximity at first encounter) and V/m (mean voltage gradient at that proximity)

source.authors: Ryan M. Kempster, Channing A. Egeberg, Nathan S. Hart, Laura Ryan, Lucille Chapuis, Caroline C. Kerr, Carl Schmidt, Charlie Huveneers, Enrico Gennari, Kara E. Yopak, Jessica J. Meeuwig, Shaun P. Collin
source.title: How Close is too Close? The Effect of a Non-Lethal Electric Shark Deterrent on White Shark Behaviour

method: field experiment with stereo-video rigs: baited target with an active versus an inactive Shark Shield Freedom7 electric deterrent; distance of closest approach measured from stereo footage
conditions: Free-ranging wild white sharks, sub-adults estimated at 2 to 4 m, at Seal Island, Mossel Bay, South Africa. 44 trials (22 control with inactive device, 22 active), 322 encounters (279 control, 43 active) from 41 individual sharks. Bait: a sealed PVC container with about 0.5 kg of sardines and fish heads about 1 m in front of the cameras at about 4 m depth, never removed, so the sharks also had chemical and visual cues and the result measures the device against a bait rather than isolating the electric sense. Four rigs deployed at once at sites at least 300 m apart, rotated randomly among sites through the day, control and active balanced over locations and times. Statistics in Minitab (proportion tests; tests weighted by encounter number or shark ID), mean +/- SE. Mean first-encounter proximity was approximately 38 (+/- 5) cm with the inactive control, and significantly further away with the active device (p <= 0.001, Results). With each subsequent encounter proximity decreased by an average of 11.6 cm, an increase in tolerance of 2.6 (+/- 0.5) V/m per encounter (abstract), yet sharks continued to be deterred from interacting for the duration of each trial; there was an 83% reduction in the proportion of sharks interacting with the bait when the device was active. The authors state that the findings give no support to the theory that electric deterrents attract sharks. The voltage gradient is not measured at the shark: probe measurements taken at 50 cm intervals from an active electrode were fitted with a curve (Harris model, Fig 7), and the 9.7 V/m is that curve's estimate at the measured proximity, not a separately measured threshold. The device discharged at 1.67 Hz with a peak voltage gradient of at least 100 V/m within 5 cm of the electrode.
quote: Upon their first observed encounter, all C. carcharias were repelled at a mean (± std. error) proximity of 131 (± 10.3) cm, which corresponded to a mean voltage gradient of 9.7 (± 0.9) V/m.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in two abutting pieces ('...proximity of 131 (± 10.3) cm,' | ' which corresponded to a mean voltage gradient of 9.7 (± 0.9) V/m.'), end verified. value: deterred by light from a high-pressure sodium street lamp from the surface waters at night (larvae in a lake)
units: categorical (depth distribution of larvae under night-time lamp light)

source.authors: Mirosław Ślusarczyk, Anna Bednarska, Marcin Lukasz Zebrowski, Joanna Tałanda
source.title: Artificial light at night bans Chaoborus from vital epilimnetic waters

method: field experiment in a lake: depth-resolved zooplankton sampling at five 5 m layers in darkness before, during and after one hour of night-time lamp light; sequence day, pre-light night, light, post-light night
conditions: Wild Chaoborus flavicans larvae in the open-water zone of Lake Ros, Poland (eutrophic, dimictic, deepest basin 31 m). Light: 70 W high-pressure sodium lamp on an anchored boat 1.5 m above the water, 250 to 450 lx at the surface under the lamp; five experimental nights for the light phase, the post-light night on three of the five. Darkness before and after the light served as the reference; fixed order, no randomisation. Daytime larvae sat at 15 to 25 m, before the light at night in the upper 0 to 10 m, and under the light peaked at 5 to 10 m, with mean depth 20.1 +/- 1.2 m by day against 9.0 +/- 0.4 m under the light; total abundance did not differ between light conditions and the depth-by-treatment interaction was significant (GLMM; the text gives no Wald chi2 or P for these effects, which sit in Table 1, not read). Light intensity at the mean population depth: Wilcoxon W = 22, p = 0.056. The same lamp attracted planktivorous fish, so the larvae's shift cannot be separated from a response to predation risk; the larvae did not descend to the anoxic hypolimnion but stayed at mid-depth, and neither the light gradient nor food distribution fully explained that residence. A laboratory anoxia test on lake-collected larvae is a separate part of the paper and is not used here. Night sonar and plankton sampling ran on five summer nights between 4 and 25 July 2019; a separate daytime sonar transect is dated 20 to 22 June 2015. Fish attraction to the lamp is described (fish appeared within seconds) but not counted or tested.
quote: Nighttime field tests revealed that light from an HPS street lamp mounted on a boat anchored in open water attracted planktivorous fish, but deterred planktonic Chaoborus from rich but risky surface waters.
note: Whole abstract sentence read in three abutting pieces ('...anchored in' | ' open water attracted planktivorous fish, but deterred planktonic Chaoborus from rich but risky' | ' surface waters.'), end verified. Species identity (Chaoborus flavicans) from the Methods and the paper's reference list. Eyed larva avoiding light, so filed under behaviour_vision; the sentence names the genus and the study species is C. flavicans. value: mean preferred body temperature 28.1 C, lower than that of Podarcis muralis in the same gradient
units: categorical (mean selected body temperature, C, in a laboratory thermal gradient)

source.authors: Jelena Ćorović, Nada Ćosić, Jelka Crnobrnja-Isailović
source.title: Comparing Preferred Temperatures and Evaporative Water Loss Rates in Two Syntopic Populations of Lacertid Lizard Species

method: laboratory thermal-gradient choice of wild-caught adult male lizards: hourly cloacal temperature across the day
conditions: Wild adult males, 10 per species, caught by noose in May 2019 on Avala mountain near Belgrade, Serbia (syntopic populations), kept individually for no more than 3 days with food and water before testing. Each lizard tested alone in a 100 x 40 x 30 cm terrarium with a single 150 W infrared reflector bulb at one end giving a gradient of roughly 20 to 45 C, room near 20 C, natural photoperiod; lights on 07:00, lizards placed at 08:00, cloacal temperature read hourly from 09:00 to 17:00; not fed during trials. Means are printed as 28.1 +/- 2.5 C (D. praticola) and 30.6 +/- 3.8 C (P. muralis); the paper does not say whether +/- is SD or SE, nor exactly how hourly readings were pooled per lizard. Set-point range (Tset, the central 50% of selected body temperatures) was 26.9 to 29.4 C in D. praticola and 29.0 to 32.7 C in P. muralis. Repeated-measures GLM: species difference F(1,18) = 18.98, p < 0.001, and Tp varied among hourly intervals, with a decreasing trend in D. praticola (F(8,144) = 2.19, p < 0.05; time x species F(8,144) = 1.19, p = 0.311); but with snout-vent length and body mass as covariates the species effect was no longer significant (F(1,16) = 1.13, p = 0.305), nor was time (F(8,128) = 0.51, p = 0.846) or time x species (F(8,128) = 1.28, p = 0.261). Trial order not stated; no control group. Males only, so no information on females or juveniles. Total evaporative water loss did not differ between species (2.76% and 2.67%, p = 0.770) and preferred temperature was not correlated with total water loss in either species.
quote: Our results show that D. praticola prefers lower temperatures (mean Tp = 28.1 °C) than P. muralis (mean Tp = 30.6 °C).
note: Whole abstract sentence; both species' values are in their own clauses and this line uses the Darevskia praticola clause. Page metadata lists CC BY 3.0; Crossref single-DOI lookup worked and lists CC BY 4.0 (content-version vor) for this DOI; authors, volume 14, issue 24 and article number 3642 match Crossref and the page. Family and order from main (docs/views/gaps, Darevskia praticola). Not on main or any desk branch (grep of ani14243642 and the species with sense_thermal). The sentence was read as one piece in the page summary and ends at the period; the same-paper line for Podarcis muralis is filed in this unit.
